topic: Microsoft Open Trust Stack for AI Agents: ASSERT + ACS + OpenInference — Production Governance Guide
keyword: Microsoft Open Trust Stack AI agent governance

key_points: Primary announcement for Microsoft's open trust stack at Build 2026.
Positions ASSERT as policy-driven evaluation and ACS as a portable runtime control standard.
Frames the workflow as evaluate with ASSERT, apply controls with ACS, re-run evaluations, then monitor production behavior.
Explains why OpenInference is the shared telemetry contract across ASSERT, ACS, and production observability.
Describes ACS checkpoints across input, LLM call, state, tool execution, and output.
Highlights the feedback loop: ASSERT reads OpenInference spans, ACS emits control-decision spans, Phoenix/Arize AX consumes the same traces.
Reference implementation for policy enforcement, identity, sandboxing, and SRE controls for autonomous agents.
Makes a production argument that prompt-level safety is advisory, while deterministic wrappers can block actions before tool execution.
Shows YAML policy patterns for deny rules and human approval requirements around high-risk actions.
Defines Foundry Agent Service as Microsoft's managed platform for building, deploying, scaling, evaluating, and monitoring agents.
Covers prompt agents, hosted agents, the Responses API, managed identity, observability, built-in tools, MCP support, and publishing paths.
Useful for tying the open trust stack into production hosting and enterprise deployment choices.
Provides a vendor-neutral security pattern for autonomous agentic systems.
Emphasizes defense in depth, evaluation/red teaming, runtime safety systems, logging, observability, explicit action schemas, and deterministic HITL.
Useful for translating ASSERT and ACS into a broader enterprise security architecture.

stats.fact: Microsoft announced the open trust stack at Build 2026 as two open-source projects: ASSERT for Adaptive Spec-driven Scoring for Evaluation and Regression Testing, and Agent Control Specification (ACS) for portable runtime controls.
Microsoft says ASSERT works across LangChain, CrewAI, LiteLLM, OpenAI, and other frameworks, and targets the 6 to 13 million generative AI developers building agents today.
ACS defines five validation checkpoints in an agent lifecycle: input, LLM, state, tool execution, and output.
Microsoft's June 2026 agentic AI failure taxonomy update adds seven new failure mode categories and is grounded in 12 months of red team engagements against deployed agentic systems.
The same Microsoft taxonomy update cites 99 CVEs in MCP-related software during 2025, plus tool poisoning moving from theory to live attack surface.
The Microsoft Agent Governance Toolkit repository states the toolkit is in public preview, supports Python 3.10+, and is designed to enforce policy around tool calls with YAML policies.
OpenInference defines a concrete attribute schema and span-kind taxonomy on top of OpenTelemetry; every OpenInference trace is a valid OTLP trace.

Foundry Agent Service includes end-to-end tracing, metrics, Application Insights integration, Microsoft Entra identity, RBAC, content filters, and virtual network isolation for enterprise agent workloads.

angles: The practical governance message is not 'use more guardrails'; it is 'turn policy into a testable and enforceable lifecycle': ASSERT before release, ACS at runtime, OpenInference everywhere.
OpenInference is the differentiator because it connects pre-production eval evidence, runtime control decisions, and production observability into one trace contract.
ACS should be explained as controls outside the model, not another prompt instruction layer; this matters for audits, approvals, and high-risk tool calls.
A production guide should map each failure class to a control location: policy evals for regressions, checkpoint controls for live actions, and traces for incident response.
The most useful implementation pattern is a progressive rollout: instrument traces first, run ASSERT on risky workflows, add ACS policies for irreversible actions, then tighten defaults.
The article can stand out by showing how Microsoft Foundry Agent Service, Agent Governance Toolkit, and third-party OpenInference tools fit together without forcing a single vendor stack.
